newsitem.title: GERMANY: Buba's Palm says investors expect punctual EMU.
newsitem.headline: Buba's Palm says investors expect punctual EMU.

text.p: Bundesbank council member Guntram Palm said on Monday investors increasingly appeared to believe European monetary union would start on time, and with a larger rather than smaller number of members.

This was partly due to a "certain tendency to qualify" the fiscal criteria for membership of the future single currency, said Palm, who is also president of the state central bank of Baden-Wuerttemberg.

In this context one had to address the question of how to deal with "more or less obvious accounting tricks" in national budgets which only served to meet the convergence criteria for the budget deficit in 1997, the key year for deciding which nations can join monetary union, Palm said.

The Maastricht Treaty states that a nation's budget deficit must not exceed three percent of gross domestic product (GDP) and its public debt must not exceed 60 percent, although it gives leeway to exceed those levels in certain circumstances.

Palm said he had always been against an excessively mechanical application of the criteria, but "manipulation" of national budgets through bookkeeping measures did not constitute a fulfilment of the criteria, according to a statement released by the state central bank.
But he added that almost all countries had significantly stepped up their efforts to consolidate their budgets "late, but perhaps not too late."
Bundesbank officials have repeatedly criticised measures taken by Italy and France to bring their budget deficits into line with EMU requirements.

France will use a special transfer from France Telecom to cover future pension liabilities to cut its deficit next year, while Italy's 1997 budget will include a one-off "tax on Europe" to ensure the country meets the criteria.
Palm said several southern European currencies, especially the Italian lira compared with the German mark, had appreciated considerably since April.
Yields on bonds in those currencies had fallen far more strongly than comparable German bond yields,
"Evidently an increasing number investors believe in a punctual start of EMU with a larger than smaller number of beginners," the statement said.

Palm also reiterated the Bundesbank's stance that the stability pact to ensure lasting budget discipline after EMU must ensure that penalties on countries exceeding the three percent limit are imposed automatically.
The circumstances under which nations could avoid such sanctions would have to be defined "precisely and restrictively," Palm said.
He added he was sure an acceptable solution could be found at the European Union summit of heads of state and government on December 13, or next year.

Germany has found itself at odds with France and most of the rest of the European Union in trying to set up very strict stability pact which will mean semi-automatic sanctions penalties for countries whose governments overspend.
Palm also said he expected the future European central bank to adopt the Bundesbank's strategy of money supply targeting.
